newsitem.title: USA: Emotional "partial birth" debate begins in Senate.
newsitem.headline: Emotional "partial birth" debate begins in Senate.

text.p: The Senate began debating the emotional and contentious ban on "partial birth" abortions Wednesday, with the measure's chief sponsor acknowledging he was five votes shy of a veto-proof victory.
Pennsylvania Republican Sen. Rick Santorum told reporters he had 62 votes in favour of the measure. To override the veto promised by President Clinton, he would need 67 votes.

The House in March passed the abortion bill by a veto-proof majority. Clinton vetoed an identical bill in 1996 and has pledged to do so again, saying the partial birth abortion ban does not allow exemptions to protect a woman's health.

"He's made it clear to the Congress that (if exemptions were made for) those exceptional circumstances where there needs to be protection for a woman's life and health, that he would support banning this procedure or banning late-term abortions," Clinton spokesman Mike McCurry said.
The White House said Clinton could back a compromise proposal drafted by Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle that allows exemptions for a woman's health.

Although most states have some restrictions on late-term or partial birth abortions, this would be the first federal legislation restricting a form of abortion since the 1973 Supreme Court decision upholding a woman's constitutional right to terminate a pregnancy.
The Senate initially expected to wrap up debate and vote by Thursday, but Santorum said the matter might spill into next week because of unrelated measures pending in the Senate.

Santorum opened the debate by showing black-and-white drawings of a foetus in the fifth month of gestation. Graphic sketches showed a pair of scissors being jammed into the foetus's skull and brains being suctioned out.
"Unfortunately, we have reached the point in our country where this is defensible," Santorum said, his voice rising to a shout. "It is killing a little baby that hasn't hurt anybody."

Santorum quoted medical authorities, including former U.S. Surgeon General C. Everett Koop, who have said the procedure is never necessary to protect the health of a woman. But those on the other side of the debate, mostly Democrats, can quote medical experts with opposing views.

California Democratic Sen. Barbara Boxer, a staunch backer of abortion rights who was the first opponent of the bill to take the floor, recounted the story of a conservative, anti-abortion woman who reluctantly underwent the procedure after problems arose in the seventh month of her third pregnancy.
The foetus had severe neurological and respiratory difficulties that could have endangered the mother and threatened her future ability to bear children, Boxer said.
"Leave us with our God, our families and our trusted medical experts," Boxer quoted the woman, Coreen Costello, as saying.

The Daschle proposal would ban all abortions after a foetus is viable, or capable of surviving outside the uterus. It would apply to the type of abortion known by its opponents as partial birth abortions as well as other surgical techniques used late in pregnancy. Exemptions would be made to save the life of a mother or for "grievous" physical health problems.

The Santorum bill, in contrast, does not address other surgical methods but would ban all partial birth abortions, before or after viability. The procedure is believed to be used in the fifth and sixth months of pregnancy.
There has been a dispute about how common the procedure is and when it is performed. Santorum cited an estimate of 5,000 cases a year.
The procedure, also referred to as dilation and extraction, involves the partial extraction of the foetus feet-first, the subsequent suctioning out of the foetal brain and the removal of the foetus.
The debate got off to an unfriendly start, with Santorum requesting that a 5 1/2-year-old girl be allowed to watch the debate from the gallery. The usual age is 6, but exceptions are common.
Boxer said she was objecting "on the basis of being a grandmother" and thought the debate inappropriate for such a young child.
